simple: a sensor that feels pushes, and also feels gravity pulling down.
analogy: the weight of the bowl shifting in Lucía's wrist.
precise: a sensor whose output is the specific force along its axis: acceleration minus gravitational acceleration, so at rest it reads 1 g directed opposite to gravity (upwards).
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: accuracy is being right on average; precision is giving the same answer every time.
analogy: a scale that is always 10 g too high is precise but not accurate.
precise: accuracy concerns the systematic error (bias, the difference between the mean reading and the true value); precision concerns the random error (spread, the standard deviation of repeated readings).
source: D3 of F0-62 (Paul Horowitz and Winfield Hill, "The Art of Electronics" (registry 4.2): measurement error, calibration, analog-to-digital conversion and quantisation error) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how common something is before you test for it.
analogy: how many afternoons out of ten bring a visitor at all.
precise: the prior probability of a condition in the population being tested; ignoring it when interpreting a test result is the base-rate fallacy.
source: D1 of F0-61 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on conditional probability (definition, Bayes' rule, law of total probability, odds form, conditional independence, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: applying Bayes' rule again and again, each new reading updating the last belief.
analogy: Samira's belief after the bark becomes her prior when the bell rings.
precise: a recursive estimator that keeps a probability distribution (belief) over states and, for each measurement z, sets belief(x) ← η · P(z | x) · belief(x), where η normalises; with motion, a prediction step comes before each update (RB302, F9-31).
source: D2 of F0-61 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics" (registry 4.7, RB302): the chapter on recursive state estimation (belief, the Bayes filter with prediction and measurement update, the door-state example) …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the recipe for turning "how likely is this clue if my idea is true" into "how likely is my idea, now that I have seen this clue".
analogy: Samira's reasoning about the barking dog.
precise: P(H | E) = P(E | H) P(H) / P(E), with P(E) from the law of total probability.
source: D1 of F0-61 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on conditional probability (definition, Bayes' rule, law of total probability, odds form, conditional independence, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a test that measures how fast something runs, done the same way every time.
analogy: Tomás's stopwatch evenings, if he ran them properly.
precise: a repeatable experiment that applies a defined workload to a system and records a performance metric (time, throughput, latency) together with the conditions of the run.
source: D1 of F2-51 (Brendan Gregg, "Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapters on methodology and on benchmarking (benchmarking activities, pitfalls of benchmarking, active benchmarking)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: Bernoulli is one yes/no trial; binomial counts the yeses in n identical, independent trials.
analogy: one cousin's coin; the number of helpers among four cousins.
precise: X ~ Bernoulli(p) takes 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1 − p. X ~ Binomial(n, p) has P(X = k) = C(n, k) pk (1 − p)n − k for k = 0, …, n.
source: D1 of F0-57 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on random variables and their distributions (PMF, CDF, Bernoulli and binomial, discrete uniform), on continuous …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a sensor's reading when the true value is zero.
analogy: a kitchen scale that shows 3 grams with nothing on it.
precise: a constant or slowly varying offset added to a sensor's output; it is estimated (calibrated) and subtracted.
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number of ways to pick k things out of n when the order does not matter.
analogy: the ways to pick three friends out of eight to wash the dishes.
precise: C(n, k) = n! / (k! (n − k)!), also written as n over k in brackets.
source: D1 of F0-56 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 textbook in the source registry, guide 4.2): the chapters on probability and counting (sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a recipe that turns two uniform random numbers into Gaussian ones.
analogy: two fair spinners combined so that their result lands in a bell shape.
precise: for independent U1, U2 uniform on (0, 1), Z = √(−2 ln U1) cos(2π U2) is standard Gaussian (and the same with sin gives a second, independent one).
source: D1 of F0-59 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on continuous random variables (the normal distribution, standardisation, the 68–95–99.7 rule, the exponential …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F0-59 (run record: Lab run of Listing 1 (gauss.cpp, seed 59) in this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined, Linux x86_64 build container, exit code 0 …)

simple: measuring something whose true value you already know, to find out how wrong the sensor is.
analogy: weighing the sealed 500 g bag of rice.
precise: determining the relation between a sensor's readings and known reference values (here: the bias, as the mean reading minus the reference), so that later readings can be corrected.
source: D3 of F0-62 (Paul Horowitz and Winfield Hill, "The Art of Electronics" (registry 4.2): measurement error, calibration, analog-to-digital conversion and quantisation error) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D2 of F0-62 (Randal W. simple: subtracting two nearly equal big numbers that each carry rounding error, so that only the error is left.
analogy: weighing a feather by weighing a truck with and without it.
precise: loss of significant digits when computing a − b with a ≈ b in floating-point arithmetic; the relative error of the difference can be huge even if a and b are accurate to many digits. MA302 treats it fully.
source: D2 of F0-58 (David Goldberg, "What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic" (ACM Computing Surveys, 1991; registry 4.1): rounding error and cancellation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F0-58 (run record: Lab run of the forensic evidence program variance_bug.cpp, same toolchain and flags, exit code 0 (variance_bug.log). simple: add up many small, independent random nudges, and the total has a bell shape, whatever the shape of the nudges.
analogy: the thermometer's wobble is the sum of many tiny electrical and air-current effects.
precise: for independent, identically distributed Xi with mean μ and finite variance σ2, the distribution of (X1 + … + Xn − nμ)/(σ√n) approaches N(0, 1) as n grows.
source: D1 of F0-59 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on continuous random variables (the normal distribution, standardisation, the 68–95–99.7 rule, the exponential …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a third thing that pushes two quantities at once, so they move together although neither pushes the other.
analogy: the one power adapter that makes both of Jonas's thermometers wobble together.
precise: a variable Z that influences both X and Y; it produces correlation between X and Y without any causal link between them.
source: D1 of F0-60 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on joint distributions (covariance and correlation, variance of sums, uncorrelated versus independent, the …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "not A": everything that is not in the event.
analogy: all the unshaded boxes.
precise: the event Ac = S minus A; P(Ac) = 1 − P(A).
source: D1 of F0-56 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 textbook in the source registry, guide 4.2): the chapters on probability and counting (sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the chance of something, given that you already know something else happened.
analogy: the chance that a visitor is at the door, given that the dog is barking.
precise: P(A | B) = P(A and B)/P(B), defined when P(B) > 0; read "probability of A given B". In general P(A | B) ≠ P(B | A).
source: D1 of F0-61 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on conditional probability (definition, Bayes' rule, law of total probability, odds form, conditional independence, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the covariance rescaled to lie between −1 and +1, so it has no units.
analogy: a score for "how neatly do the notebook's dots line up?".
precise: ρ = Cov(X, Y)/(σXσY), estimated from data by r = sxy/(sxsy) (Pearson's correlation coefficient). |r| = 1 exactly when the points lie on a straight line; r measures linear association only.
source: D1 of F0-60 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on joint distributions (covariance and correlation, variance of sums, uncorrelated versus independent, the …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a number that is positive when two quantities tend to be above their averages at the same time, negative when one tends to be above while the other is below.
analogy: sunshine and kitchen warmth going up together.
precise: Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μX)(Y − μY)] = E[XY] − μXμY; from data, sxy = Σ(xi − x̄)(yi − ȳ)/(n − 1). Its unit is the product of the two units. Cov(X, X) = Var(X).
source: D1 of F0-60 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on joint distributions (covariance and correlation, variance of sums, uncorrelated versus independent, the …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a table holding all the variances and covariances of several quantities at once.
analogy: one page of Hana's notebook that summarises how every column wobbles and how every pair of columns moves together.
precise: for a random vector (X1, …, Xk), the k × k matrix Σ with entries Σij = Cov(Xi, Xj); the diagonal holds the variances, and Σ is symmetric (MA201 F0-51, transpose).
source: D1 of F0-60 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on joint distributions (covariance and correlation, variance of sums, uncorrelated versus independent, the …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D2 of F0-60 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics" (registry 4.7, RB302): covariance matrices of robot state estimates and the Kalman gain) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the probability of getting this value or less.
analogy: stacking the bars from the left and reading the height of the stack so far.
precise: F(x) = P(X ≤ x), defined for every real x; it rises from 0 to 1 and never goes down. P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a).
source: D1 of F0-57 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on random variables and their distributions (PMF, CDF, Bernoulli and binomial, discrete uniform), on continuous …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far one value is from the mean, with a sign.
analogy: "this morning was 7 seconds slower than usual".
precise: xi − x̄; the deviations of a data set always add up to 0.
source: D1 of F0-58 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on expectation (definition, linearity, variance, Bernoulli and binomial moments), the chapters on joint …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: discrete ones take separate values you can list (0, 1, 2, …); continuous ones can take any value in a range.
analogy: the number of helpers versus the exact time the kettle takes to boil.
precise: X is discrete if its possible values form a finite or countable list; X is continuous if it has a probability density function (below), so that every single value has probability 0.
source: D1 of F0-57 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on random variables and their distributions (PMF, CDF, Bernoulli and binomial, discrete uniform), on continuous …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: events that can never happen at the same time.
analogy: "total 7" and "a double" (two equal faces): no box is both.
precise: events A and B with no outcome in common (A and B = ∅). Also called mutually exclusive.
source: D1 of F0-56 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 textbook in the source registry, guide 4.2): the chapters on probability and counting (sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the full description of which values a random variable takes and how often.
analogy: the shape of Mei's scoreboard bars after many evenings.
precise: the assignment of probabilities P(X ∈ A) to sets A of values; it is fixed by the PMF (discrete), the PDF (continuous) or the CDF (both).
source: D1 of F0-57 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on random variables and their distributions (PMF, CDF, Bernoulli and binomial, discrete uniform), on continuous …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the angle error that keeps growing when you add up turning rates.
analogy: after spinning slowly for a long time, Lucía no longer knows which way she faces.
precise: the growth of error in an angle obtained by integrating rate measurements; a constant bias b produces an error b·t that grows linearly with time, and noise adds a random walk.
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); R2 of F1-65 (lab run of the university's model, g++ 13.3.0) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a ready-made function that gives Gaussian probabilities, because the bell's area has no simple formula.
analogy: a measuring cup already marked for the bell shape.
precise: erf(x) = (2/√π) × the area under exp(−t2) from 0 to x; P(|Z| < k) = erf(k/√2). C++ provides std::erf and std::erfc = 1 − erf in <cmath>.
source: D1 of F0-59 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on continuous random variables (the normal distribution, standardisation, the 68–95–99.7 rule, the exponential …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D2 of F0-59 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (registry 4.1): the <cmath> functions erf, erfc, exp, log, cos; the random number generation clause (mt19937 specified exactly; distributions such as normal_distribution specified by their …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a group of outcomes you care about, such as "the total is 7".
analogy: the boxes Amina shaded on her paper.
precise: a subset A of the sample space; A "happens" when the outcome lies in A.
source: D1 of F0-56 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 textbook in the source registry, guide 4.2): the chapters on probability and counting (sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the long-run average value of a random variable.
analogy: the balance point of the scoreboard bars of F0-57 if they were weights on a ruler.
precise: for a discrete X, E[X] = Σ x · P(X = x) over all possible x; written μ (mu). For a fair die, E[X] = (1 + 2 + … + 6)/6 = 3.5, a value the die itself never shows.
source: D1 of F0-58 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on expectation (definition, linearity, variance, Bernoulli and binomial moments), the chapters on joint …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 of F0-58 (run record: Lab run of checks.cpp (recomputes every number in the text), same toolchain and flags, exit code 0 (checks.log))

simple: the number of ways to put n different things in a row.
analogy: the ways to line up four different cups on a shelf.
source: D1 of F0-56 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 textbook in the source registry, guide 4.2): the chapters on probability and counting (sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the smooth, symmetric hill shape that many measurements make when you draw their histogram.
analogy: the thermometer readings piling up around the true room temperature, fewer and fewer further out.
precise: the continuous distribution N(μ, σ2) with density f(x) = exp(−(x − μ)2/(2σ2)) / (σ√(2π)); its mean is μ and its standard deviation σ.
source: D1 of F0-59 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on continuous random variables (the normal distribution, standardisation, the 68–95–99.7 rule, the exponential …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a sensor that measures how fast it is turning.
analogy: Lucía feeling herself turn the corner.
precise: a sensor whose output is the angular rate about its axis, in degrees or radians per second; MEMS gyros used in IMUs measure rate, not angle.
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a bar chart of how many data values fall into each of several equal ranges (bins).
analogy: Mei's scoreboard bars.
precise: for bins [bi, bi+1) covering the data, the counts ni; dividing by N gives frequencies (estimates of probabilities) and dividing by N × width gives a density estimate. Every value must fall into exactly one bin.
source: D1 of F0-57 (Joseph K. simple: a small chip that feels tilting, pushing and turning.
analogy: Lucía's wrist and her sense of turning while she carries the soup.
precise: a sensor package that measures specific force with accelerometers and angular rate with gyroscopes, usually along three perpendicular axes each; a magnetometer is often added. (The F9 courses use the registered analogy "the balance sense in your inner ear", analogy registry.)
source: D1 of F1-65 (Randal W. Beard, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: knowing that one happened does not change the chance of the other.
analogy: the red die does not know what the blue die did.
precise: A and B are independent when P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
source: D1 of F0-56 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 textbook in the source registry, guide 4.2): the chapters on probability and counting (sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: taking turns: A, B, A, B, instead of all A first and then all B.
analogy: Nadia and Samir walking their routes on the same mornings, so a rainy week slows both.
precise: alternating the measurements of the versions being compared, so that slow changes of the machine (other load, temperature, frequency) affect both versions alike instead of biasing one.
source: D3 of F0-63 (Brendan Gregg, "Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud" (cited by SP302 F2-51 as its D1): the chapters on methodology and on benchmarking (variation, warm-up, pitfalls of benchmarking, statistics of latency)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the average of many independent repeats gets closer and closer to the expected value.
analogy: after a year of mornings, Ravi's average kettle time hardly changes when one more morning is added.
precise: for independent, identically distributed Xi with mean μ, the sample mean x̄n converges to μ as n grows.
source: D1 of F0-58 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on expectation (definition, linearity, variance, Bernoulli and binomial moments), the chapters on joint …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: add up all the separate ways something can happen.
analogy: the dog barks either because of a visitor or because of something else; the total barking is both added.
precise: if H and not-H split all possibilities, P(E) = P(E | H) P(H) + P(E | not H) P(not H); more generally the sum over any partition.
source: D1 of F0-61 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on conditional probability (definition, Bayes' rule, law of total probability, odds form, conditional independence, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a formula that says how a reading is made from the true value plus errors.
analogy: "what the scale shows = what the rice weighs + 10 g + a flicker".
precise: z = x + b + n, where x is the true value, b the bias, n zero-mean random noise (often modelled as Gaussian with standard deviation σ); real sensors add quantisation and range limits.
source: D1 of F0-62 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics" (registry 4.7, RB302): measurement models with additive Gaussian noise; measurement noise covariance in the Kalman filter) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D2 of F0-62 (Randal W. simple: the median is the middle value after sorting; the 90th percentile is the value that 90 % of results are at or below.
analogy: line up all of Tomás's omelette times from fastest to slowest and point at the middle one.
precise: for n sorted values, the median is the value at position (n+1)/2 for odd n (the mean of the two middle values for even n); the nearest-rank p-th percentile is the value at rank ⌈p/100 × n⌉.
source: D4 of F2-51 (MA202 Probability and statistics, chapter F0-63 "Statistics for benchmarks: median, percentiles, outliers" (this university; course card in guide section 5). simple: odds compare "yes" to "no" (1 to 9); the likelihood ratio says how many times better the clue fits "yes" than "no".
analogy: barking is 4.5 times more common with a visitor than without.
precise: odds(H) = P(H)/P(not H); likelihood ratio = P(E | H)/P(E | not H); Bayes' rule in odds form: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio.
source: D1 of F0-61 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on conditional probability (definition, Bayes' rule, law of total probability, odds form, conditional independence, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an outcome is one possible result; the sample space is the list of all of them.
analogy: one box of Amina's six-by-six square; the whole square.
precise: the sample space S is the set of all possible outcomes of the experiment; an outcome is an element of S. For two dice, S has 36 outcomes (red value, blue value).
source: D1 of F0-56 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 textbook in the source registry, guide 4.2): the chapters on probability and counting (sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F0-56 (run record: Lab run of Listing 1 (dice_count.cpp) in this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined, Linux x86_64 build container, exit code 0 …)

simple: an outlier is a value far from the others; the fences are a rule for "far".
analogy: the morning the level crossing was closed.
precise: a value below q1 − 1.5·IQR or above q3 + 1.5·IQR is flagged as an outlier; the factor 1.5 is a convention, not a law. A flag means "investigate", not "delete".
source: D2 of F0-63 (John W. Tukey, "Exploratory Data Analysis": box plots, quartiles ("hinges") and the fences for outlying values) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two numbers measured together each time, drawn as one dot per pair.
analogy: each line of Hana's notebook: sunshine and temperature on the same afternoon.
precise: observations (xi, yi), i = 1 … n, of two random variables X and Y; the scatter plot puts a point at each (xi, yi).
source: D1 of F0-60 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on joint distributions (covariance and correlation, variance of sums, uncorrelated versus independent, the …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "Out of a hundred".
analogy: Pretending the bread was cut into 100 tiny equal slices and counting how many you ate.
precise: p % means p/100; 37.5 % = 0.375 = 3/8. Percentages above 100 are allowed.
source: D1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run)

simple: what you believed before the clue; how well the clue fits each possibility; what you believe after.
analogy: "visitors are rare"; "the dog barks at 9 out of 10 visitors but also often at nothing"; "now I think a visitor is fairly likely".
precise: the prior is P(H); the likelihood is P(E | H) viewed as a function of the hypothesis H; the posterior is P(H | E).
source: D1 of F0-61 (Joseph K. simple: a number from 0 (never) to 1 (always) that says how likely an event is.
analogy: the share of the drawer's socks that are red, if you grab one without looking.
precise: a function P that gives every event A a number P(A) with P(A) ≥ 0, P(S) = 1, and P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) when A and B cannot happen together. When all outcomes are equally likely, P(A) = (outcomes in A) / (outcomes in S).
source: D1 of F0-56 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 textbook in the source registry, guide 4.2): the chapters on probability and counting (sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: for continuous values, how much probability there is per unit of the value, like people per square metre.
analogy: how crowded the scoreboard would look if you made the bars infinitely thin.
precise: a function f(x) ≥ 0 with total area 1 such that P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the area under f between a and b. A density value can be larger than 1; an area cannot.
source: D1 of F0-57 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on random variables and their distributions (PMF, CDF, Bernoulli and binomial, discrete uniform), on continuous …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a table: each possible value and its probability.
analogy: the bars, scaled so that all bars together make 1.
precise: p(x) = P(X = x) for a discrete X; p(x) ≥ 0 and the p(x) over all possible x add up to 1.
source: D1 of F0-57 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on random variables and their distributions (PMF, CDF, Bernoulli and binomial, discrete uniform), on continuous …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: A recipe that produces numbers that look random.
analogy: A very long, fixed shuffled list of numbers that you start reading at some place.
precise: An algorithm that produces a sequence of numbers from a starting value (the seed); the same seed gives the same sequence, as R3 shows with seed 2026. This course uses std::mt19937 with std::uniform_int_distribution.
source: R3 of F0-38, D2 of F0-38 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1)

simple: the quartiles cut the sorted list into four equal parts; the IQR is the width of the middle half.
analogy: "on a normal half of the mornings, the walk takes between 12.1 and 12.9 minutes".
precise: in this course, q1 is the nearest-rank 25th percentile and q3 the nearest-rank 75th percentile; IQR = q3 − q1. Other tools use other quartile rules (unverified box).
source: D1 of F0-63 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 course textbook): medians and quantiles, skewness, order statistics) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D2 of F0-63 (John W. Tukey, "Exploratory Data Analysis": box plots, quartiles ("hinges") and the fences for outlying values) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: anything you can repeat whose result you cannot predict exactly, such as rolling a die.
analogy: Leo's roll on games evening.
precise: a procedure with a well-defined set of possible results, exactly one of which occurs each time it is performed.
source: D1 of F0-56 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 textbook in the source registry, guide 4.2): the chapters on probability and counting (sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a number that depends on how a random experiment turns out.
analogy: the number Mei writes on the scoreboard after the coin tosses.
precise: a function X from the sample space S to the real numbers; X(s) is the value for outcome s. Written with a capital letter; its possible values with small letters (X = k).
source: D1 of F0-57 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on random variables and their distributions (PMF, CDF, Bernoulli and binomial, discrete uniform), on continuous …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the smallest step the sensor can show, and the rounding error that the steps add.
analogy: a scale that shows whole grams only.
precise: a quantiser maps a value to the nearest multiple of its step Δ; when the input varies over many steps, the rounding error is close to uniform on [−Δ/2, Δ/2] and has standard deviation Δ/√12.
source: D3 of F0-62 (Paul Horowitz and Winfield Hill, "The Art of Electronics" (registry 4.2): measurement error, calibration, analog-to-digital conversion and quantisation error) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F0-62 (run record: Lab run of Listing 3 (noise_avg.cpp), same toolchain and flags, exit code 0 (noise_avg.log))

simple: a summary number that a few strange values cannot move much.
analogy: one closed crossing changes Samir's average but not his middle value.
precise: a statistic whose value changes little when a small fraction of the data is replaced by arbitrary values; the median and the IQR are robust, the mean and the standard deviation are not.
source: D1 of F0-63 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 course textbook): medians and quantiles, skewness, order statistics) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D2 of F0-63 (John W. Tukey, "Exploratory Data Analysis": box plots, quartiles ("hinges") and the fences for outlying values) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the same program, run again on the same machine, takes a different time.
analogy: the omelette takes longer when other cooks share the stove.
precise: the spread of repeated measurements of an unchanged workload, caused by everything the program does not control: other processes, interrupts, frequency changes, cache and memory state, timer resolution. In this chapter it is reported as (max − min) / median.
source: D1 of F2-51 (Brendan Gregg, "Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapters on methodology and on benchmarking (benchmarking activities, pitfalls of benchmarking, active benchmarking)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 of F2-51 (run record: lab runs of Listing 5 (noise_quiet.log, noise_busy.log), same toolchain, exit code 0; measurements of a shared cloud virtual machine)

simple: the ordinary average of measured numbers.
analogy: Ravi's ten kettle times added up and divided by ten.
precise: x̄ = (x1 + … + xn)/n; an estimate of E[X] computed from data.
source: D1 of F0-58 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on expectation (definition, linearity, variance, Bernoulli and binomial moments), the chapters on joint …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: when the quantity is bigger than a sensor can measure, the sensor keeps reporting its largest (or smallest) possible reading.
analogy: a measuring jug that is full: pour in more and it still shows "full".
precise: the condition in which the input is outside the measurable range, so the output stays at the end code of the converter; also called clipping. Saturated readings are not the true value.
source: D2 of F0-57 (Paul Horowitz and Winfield Hill, "The Art of Electronics" (registry 4.2): analog-to-digital conversion, code range and saturation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how often a detector catches a real problem; how often it complains when there is none.
analogy: how often the dog barks at a real visitor; how often it barks at nothing.
precise: sensitivity (true-positive rate) = P(alarm | condition); false-alarm rate (false-positive rate) = P(alarm | no condition); 1 − false-alarm rate is called specificity.
source: D1 of F0-61 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on conditional probability (definition, Bayes' rule, law of total probability, odds form, conditional independence, …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: small random wobbles in a sensor's readings.
analogy: the line looking slightly different every time a cloud moves.
precise: the part of a measurement that differs from the true value in ways that change from reading to reading; real sensors always have some.
source: D3 of F9-02 (pending verification)

simple: a distribution with a long tail on one side.
analogy: a walk can be a few minutes slower than usual for many reasons, but it cannot be much faster than the fastest possible pace.
precise: a distribution that is not symmetric about its centre; timings are right-skewed: bounded below by the time the work needs, with a tail of slow runs caused by interference. In a right-skewed sample the mean lies above the median.
source: D1 of F0-63 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (the MA202 course textbook): medians and quantiles, skewness, order statistics) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D3 of F0-63 (Brendan Gregg, "Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud" (cited by SP302 F2-51 as its D1): the chapters on methodology and on benchmarking (variation, warm-up, pitfalls of benchmarking, statistics of latency)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the typical distance of a value from the mean, in the same units as the data.
analogy: "the kettle is usually within a few seconds of its average".
precise: σ = √Var(X); from data, s = √s2. Abbreviated sd or std dev.
source: D1 of F0-58 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on expectation (definition, linearity, variance, Bernoulli and binomial moments), the chapters on joint …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much the average itself would wobble if you repeated the whole set of measurements.
analogy: Ravi's ten-morning average changes a little from one fortnight to the next, much less than single mornings do.
precise: for n independent readings each with standard deviation σ, the mean has standard deviation σ/√n; estimated by s/√n.
source: D1 of F0-58 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on expectation (definition, linearity, variance, Bernoulli and binomial moments), the chapters on joint …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F0-58 (run record: Lab run of Listing 2 (mean_of_n.cpp, seed 58), same toolchain and flags, exit code 0 (mean_of_n.log))

simple: the Gaussian with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, the "unit" bell.
analogy: the thermometer's wobble measured in "wobble units" instead of degrees.
precise: Z ~ N(0, 1); its CDF is written Φ(z) and equals (1 + erf(z/√2))/2.
source: D1 of F0-59 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on continuous random variables (the normal distribution, standardisation, the 68–95–99.7 rule, the exponential …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D2 of F0-59 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (registry 4.1): the <cmath> functions erf, erfc, exp, log, cos; the random number generation clause (mt19937 specified exactly; distributions such as normal_distribution specified by their …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the far ends of the hill, where values are rare.
analogy: the afternoon reading that is unusually high.
precise: the probability P(X > t) (upper tail) or P(X < −t) (lower tail) for large t. A distribution is heavy-tailed when its tails fall much more slowly than a Gaussian's with the same σ.
source: D1 of F0-59 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on continuous random variables (the normal distribution, standardisation, the 68–95–99.7 rule, the exponential …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: uncorrelated means "no straight-line tendency"; independent means "knowing one tells you nothing at all about the other".
analogy: the height of a ball thrown up and down is fully determined by time, yet over a symmetric flight it is uncorrelated with the time measured from the top.
precise: independence implies Cov = 0; Cov = 0 does not imply independence (example: Y = X2 with X symmetric about 0).
source: D1 of F0-60 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on joint distributions (covariance and correlation, variance of sums, uncorrelated versus independent, the …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F0-60 (run record: Lab run of Listing 2 (corr_demo.cpp, seed 60), same toolchain and flags, exit code 0 (corr_demo.log))

simple: every value in a range is equally likely.
analogy: the moment the washing machine finishes, if all you know is "some time in the next 20 minutes".
precise: discrete uniform on {a, …, b}: each value has probability 1/(b − a + 1). Continuous uniform on [a, b]: density 1/(b − a) inside the interval and 0 outside.
source: D1 of F0-57 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on random variables and their distributions (PMF, CDF, Bernoulli and binomial, discrete uniform), on continuous …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the average of the squared distances from the mean: a measure of spread.
analogy: how wobbly the kettle is, measured in "seconds squared".
precise: Var(X) = E[(X − μ)2] = E[X2] − μ2, written σ2. From data: s2 = Σ(xi − x̄)2/(n − 1) (sample variance) or the same sum divided by n.
source: D1 of F0-58 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapter on expectation (definition, linearity, variance, Bernoulli and binomial moments), the chapters on joint …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a run you do first and do not count.
analogy: preheating the stove before the timed omelette.
precise: an untimed execution of the workload before measurement, so that one-time costs (first touch of memory pages, filling caches, loading code, the processor changing its clock speed) do not land in the timed runs.
source: D1 of F2-51 (Brendan Gregg, "Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapters on methodology and on benchmarking (benchmarking activities, pitfalls of benchmarking, active benchmarking)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 of F2-51 (run record: lab runs of Listing 5 (noise_quiet.log, noise_busy.log), same toolchain, exit code 0; measurements of a shared cloud virtual machine)

simple: how many standard deviations a value is above (positive) or below (negative) the mean.
analogy: "this reading is two wobbles too high".
precise: z = (x − μ)/σ; if X ~ N(μ, σ2), then Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1).
source: D1 of F0-59 (Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, "Introduction to Probability" (MA202 textbook, guide 4.2): the chapters on continuous random variables (the normal distribution, standardisation, the 68–95–99.7 rule, the exponential …) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
